Peak Poker Performance

   Once you become aware of your patterns, you can begin to make
some changes. If an unhelpful thought comes into your mind, you can la-
bel it as such and let it pass. Thoughts are much like clouds in the sky –
they pop into our awareness and can just float on by – unless we choose
to attend to them in some way. This pattern of thinking and attending
that I’m describing is known as mindfulness, and it’s definitely a tool that
you want in your peak performance tool kit. I’ll have more to say about
mindfulness in the next chapter.

Summary
This chapter explored several common mental game leaks and I’m sure
you noticed that they are not completely separate from one another.
Strong emotions elicit several reactions, which can include rumination,
self-criticism, avoidance, and emotion-driven behaviors. Often, we enact
thoughts and behaviors that are not especially helpful. Being aware of po-
tential leaks is one of the first steps to implementing a peak performance
strategy, so I hope you’ll take the time to use the tracking tools to in-
crease your awareness of any potential leaks you might be falling victim
to.

Chapter Highlights
   ♠ Fear is at the root of many mental game issues.
   ♠ Emotion-driven behavior is also something to be on guard for.
   ♠ Self-awareness is a key to increasing peak performance.
   ♠ It is not necessary or even possible to eliminate emotions; they
       simply must be managed.
   ♠ Self-criticism, rumination, avoidance and emotion-driven
       behaviors are common psychological hurdles.

                                         Common Psychological Hurdles

Jonathan’s Comments
When I first started playing poker, I had a terrible problem with rumina-
tion. For example, when I would get all-in with 80% equity five times in a
row and lose all five, I would start questioning how I could possibly be so
unlucky. After playing poker for a few years, I came to the realization that
if you play a lot of poker, as I did, you are bound to go through both in-
credibly lucky and unlucky stretches. Once I accepted that short-term
variance is out of my control and therefore completely irrelevant, my ru-
mination problem naturally disappeared.
    Today, the only time I find myself ruminating is after I make a horrible
mistake. Fortunately, these situations don’t occur too often. My rumina-
tion seems to be a form of self-criticism. When I hear my subconscious
berating me for my poor play, I write the poor play in my notebook and
resolve to address the situation after my session, away from the table.
After writing the mistake down, I am usually able to direct my attention
back to the game. While this tactic of reviewing my mistakes later may
seem like a form of avoidance, it doesn’t seem to affect me in a negative
way. I have found that when something is not fully addressed in my mind,
I ruminate on it, but as soon as I write it down and know I will review it in
the future, I forget about it. If you ruminate over your mistakes, try writ-
ing them down and see how it works for you.
    Similar to my propensity to ruminate as a young poker player, I also
had intense emotional reactions when things went poorly. Once, I lost 12
out of 16 SnG tournaments within five minutes of starting the games. I
slammed my mouse down on a glass dining room table and it shattered all
over me. Instead of cleaning it up, I continued playing my four remaining
games. I somehow managed to win the remaining four games to break
even for the 16-game set. Talk about lucky! I was only down the cost of
the table.
    While I am not sure if having shattered glass all over my lap provided a
wake-up call, my emotions do not elicit destructive behavior anymore.
When things go poorly in live poker, I remain completely stoic and usually
feel no reaction at all, likely because it takes way more than a few nega-

   Never put off till tomorrow what may be done the day after tomorrow

   Procrastination is one of the most common mental game issues players
(and the general public) face today. Studies show that as many as 95% of
people in the United States admit to procrastinating with 20% being ac-
curately classified as chronic procrastinators. It shouldn’t be too surprising
then that almost all of the poker players I consult with have at least some
issues with procrastination. The top two procrastination problems I en-
counter are players not putting in enough volume and not studying
enough.

ways. For the sake of this discussion, I’m going to define procrastination
as the voluntary delay of an intended action. Not all delays can be classi-
fied as procrastination. If you put off a study session because a family
member got sick and needed your help, that’s not procrastination. Some-

Peak Poker Performance

times things come up and we have to rearrange our schedules and put
things off until a later time. Procrastination is when we put something off
that we know we should be doing; it’s a needless delay. It’s like we have
an inner five year old that takes hold, stomps a foot, and declares “I don’t
want to do hand history reviews.” Typically, it feels good in the moment
to put off doing something we don’t feel like doing, but in the long run it
leads to guilt, anxiety, stress, and less than stellar results. In essence, pro-
crastination shapes us into being our own worst enemy.
   My goal with this chapter is to give you a number of strategies and
mindset shifts that you can choose from to beat procrastination. I’m go-
ing to summarize the most salient research on the topic and I’ll list a num-
ber of tried and true tactics and remedies that have the most empirical
support. If you are willing to take action on some of this information, I’m
confident that you can reduce the amount of time you spend procrasti-
nating and start getting things done.

Why Procrastinate?
People have all sorts of ideas to address why we procrastinate and what
should be done to stop it. Unfortunately, most of what we think we know
about how to behave most efficiently is wrong. Procrastination is a multi-
faceted topic. It involves a variety of emotions, thoughts, attitudes, skills,
and forces that we are unaware of. Furthermore, the reasons we procras-
tinate vary from person to person and even from situation to situation.
We get started right away on some tasks and delay interminably on oth-
ers. Let’s see if we can’t get a better handle on why we procrastinate in
this section.
   Dr. Timothy Pychyl is one of the world’s leading researchers on pro-
crastination. He says it’s a curious phenomenon because we do it to make
our lives more pleasant but it ends up causing us pain in the form of
stress. The wisest course of action would be to do the offensive task as
soon as humanly possible, but that’s not what most of us do. Instead, Py-
chyl says we are most likely to procrastinate on tasks that we view as
aversive or unpleasant. It’s important to note that what one person finds

                                                  Beating Procrastination

aversive, another may not. Some people have no trouble studying, while
others think it’s the most painful thing in the world. We are more likely to
find a task aversive if we perceive it as:

   ♠ boring
   ♠ frustrating
   ♠ difficult
   ♠ ambiguous (we don’t know what to do or where to start)
   ♠ overwhelming
   ♠ unstructured
   ♠ non-meaningful.

    When you feel pressure to do a task that has a lot of the above com-
ponents, you are more likely to have a strong negative visceral reaction to
it. The more negative emotions you feel about a particular task, the more
likely you are to put it off. In his research, Pychyl found that chronic pro-
crastinators put off tasks as a means of what he calls mood repair. In
other words, just thinking about doing the task made them feel bad, so
they put it off in order to feel better.
    If you really want the perfect procrastination storm, put yourself in a
situation where you face an aversive task and you have lots of freedom.
Make sure there’s no deadline for good measure. If you add a touch of fear
of failure on top, there’s a good chance you’ll never get anything done!

Peak Poker Performance



         (Expectancy x Value)/(Impulsiveness x Delay)


    Let’s unpack the four variables so you can see how they work together
to produce procrastination.
    Expectancy describes how often you expect to be successful. Do you
have a lot of confidence in your ability to accomplish what you need to? If
so you are said to be high in expectancy. If you are high in expectancy,
you are more likely to get to work. If you are low in expectancy, you do
not have much confidence in your ability and you may feel increased
stress, anxiety and/or fear around the task. As expected, people who are
low in expectancy are more likely to procrastinate.
    There is a strong correlation between expectancy and procrastination.
People often think that procrastinators are over-confident, but research
shows that they are often low in expectancy. If you think that you are not
likely to succeed or if you don’t know how to do something, you are more
likely to procrastinate. Increase your expectancy or confidence, and you’ll
decrease procrastination on average.
    Value is a measure of enjoyment or desire you have for a task. If you
expect a task to be unpleasant it holds low value to you. The top reason
most students give for procrastinating on completing term papers is that
they don’t like writing them and place a low value on this activity. People
naturally put off doing things they detest and complete those things they
like and enjoy promptly. Things that are boring are also low in value. If you
value a goal enough to be fired up about it, your value will increase. If a
task is something you think you “should” do, it’s likely to be low in value.
Look for ways to increase value and you’ll decrease procrastination.
    Do not under-estimate how important value is. As sport psychologist
Kenneth Baum describes it, “Weak desires generate weak results” (1999).
He goes on to say that all great achievements start with desire, which he
calls a dominating dream. Is improving your game or playing at a higher
level one of your most closely held values? Surprisingly, most of us never

                                                   Beating Procrastination

take the time to consider deeply what is of highest value to us. Instead,
most of us go through life following the same routines, day after day.
Take a minute to consider:

   ♠ What’s most important to you?
   ♠ What do you want your life to be about?
   ♠ What sort of person do you want to become?
   ♠ What would you like to channel your time and energy into doing?
   ♠ What role does poker play in helping you to achieve the things you
       value?


    Dr. Steel explains that Expectancy x Value is a classic economics for-
mula that elegantly summarizes how people make choices based on how
much pleasure they expect to receive and the degree of certainty that
they will receive it. This formula sums up rational behavior very well, but it
does not account for irrational behavior like procrastination so well. Steel
contends that this formula can be improved by adding the time and im-
pulsivity variables (Impulsiveness x Delay).
    Delay is the variable that relates to time. It’s human nature to value
rewards that can be realized quickly. When we have a delay, we tend to
put things off; the greater the delay, the less our motivation. In other
words, if a pay-off for a behavior is off in the distance, we’re more likely
to put it off. We tend to be more motivated by pressing deadlines.
    Impulsiveness is a personality trait. Scores of research studies show
that people who score highly on impulsiveness are also high in procrasti-
nation. Impulsive people tend to be highly distractible, lack conscientious-
ness, and are low in self-control. All those traits add up to a person who is
likely to procrastinate.
